name: Local Kurtosis Map
description: Creates spatial maps of local kurtosis values — AI-generated content often shows abnormal kurtosis distribution.
mechanism:
This method computes spatially-varying kurtosis maps to detect statistical irregularities indicative of AI generation or image manipulation:

1. **Sliding Window Kurtosis Computation**: A sliding window of size W×W (typically 16×16 or 32×32) moves across the image. For each window position, the excess kurtosis κ is computed as κ = μ₄/σ⁴ − 3, where μ₄ is the fourth central moment and σ is the standard deviation of pixel intensities within the window. Natural images typically exhibit leptokurtic distributions (κ > 0) in textured regions and near-Gaussian distributions (κ ≈ 0) in smooth regions.

2. **Multi-Channel Kurtosis Analysis**: The kurtosis map is computed independently for each color channel (R, G, B) and for luminance (Y). In natural photographs, inter-channel kurtosis differences follow predictable patterns governed by sensor noise and demosaicing. AI-generated images often show unusually uniform kurtosis across channels or abnormal inter-channel kurtosis ratios, particularly in shadow and highlight regions.

3. **Kurtosis Gradient Analysis**: The spatial gradient of the kurtosis map is computed using Sobel operators. In authentic images, kurtosis transitions occur at semantic boundaries (edges between objects) and follow content-driven patterns. AI-generated images exhibit smoother kurtosis gradients with fewer sharp transitions, reflecting the GAN/diffusion model's tendency to produce statistically homogeneous textures.

4. **Anomaly Detection via Distribution Fitting**: The global distribution of local kurtosis values is fitted to a generalized Gaussian distribution (GGD). The shape parameter β of the GGD characterizes the image type: natural photos typically yield β ∈ [0.3, 0.8], while AI-generated images tend toward β > 1.0 due to their more Gaussian-like local statistics. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares the observed kurtosis distribution against the expected natural image model.
parameters:
Window size: 16×16 or 32×32 pixels
Stride: 8 pixels (50% overlap for 16×16 window)
Color channels: R, G, B, Y (luminance)
GGD shape parameter threshold: β = 1.0
KS test significance level: α = 0.05
Minimum image size: 128×128 pixels
accuracy: 78–86% accuracy for AI-generated image detection. Kurtosis-based features achieve AUC of 0.89 on ProGAN-generated faces. Manipulation detection (splicing) achieves F1-score of 0.81. Performance degrades on heavily JPEG-compressed images (Q < 50). Best results when combined with skewness and variance maps.
source: Lyu, S. & Farid, H. (2006). Steganalysis Using Higher-Order Image Statistics. IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 1(1), 111–119.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated images through statistical texture analysis. Identifying spliced regions with different noise or texture characteristics. Steganalysis — detecting hidden data that alters local kurtosis patterns. Quality assessment — mapping regions with unusual statistical properties.
strengths:
• Kurtosis is sensitive to subtle statistical differences invisible to human observers
• Multi-channel analysis captures inter-channel inconsistencies specific to AI generation
• Computationally efficient — O(N) with integral image optimization
• Robust to geometric transformations (rotation, scaling)
• Provides interpretable spatial visualization of anomalies
limitations:
• Kurtosis is sensitive to JPEG compression artifacts — may produce false positives
• Highly textured regions naturally show high kurtosis variance, reducing discriminative power
• Modern diffusion models (DALL-E 3, Midjourney v5) produce increasingly natural kurtosis distributions
• Window size selection affects granularity — small windows are noisy, large windows lose localization
• Not effective on uniformly smooth images (e.g., synthetic gradients)

references.title: Lyu, S. & Farid, H. — Steganalysis Using Higher-Order Image Statistics (2006)
